findings.title: create() panics on the quota for any owner not yet tracked
findings.description: `*self.quota.get_mut(owner).unwrap() += 1;` panics whenever the owner has no entry in the `quota` map. The map starts empty and is never seeded, so the first link created for an owner panics here, and because the entry is never added, every later create for that owner panics too. The link is already inserted on line 47 before the panic, so the store mutates but the client gets no response and the quota stays inconsistent. POST /links is unusable for every owner.

findings.title: resolve() treats valid links as expired and vice-versa
findings.description: `expired` is set to `SystemTime::now() < link.expires_at`, which is true while the link is still VALID. The code then does `if expired { remove; return None }`, so a valid link is deleted and 404'd on access, while an expired link (now >= expires_at) falls through and resolves, counting a hit. The /l redirect returns 404 for live codes and deletes them, and serves dead ones — the opposite of the documented behavior.

findings.title: bearer_token() reads parts[1] without a length check
findings.description: `let parts: Vec<&str> = header.split(' ').collect(); parts[1].to_string();` panics with an out-of-bounds index whenever the header has fewer than two space-separated tokens. With no Authorization header, handle() passes an empty string (main.rs:91-92), which splits to a one-element vec, so parts[1] panics. This runs on every request before routing, so any unauthenticated or malformed-authorization request crashes the handler thread instead of returning 401.

findings.title: page() computes an out-of-bounds end index
findings.description: When `offset + size` exceeds the number of links, `end` is set to `all.len() + 1`, so `all[offset..end]` indexes past the end and panics. This hits the normal listing cases: GET /links with the default size 20 and fewer than 20 links stored, and GET /report (page(0, 1000)) with fewer than 1000 links.

findings.title: add_resolved() does a non-atomic read-modify-write
findings.description: `add_resolved` loads the counter, adds 1 in a local, and stores it back — a non-atomic RMW on an AtomicI64. Concurrent handler threads (each calls it on every redirect) can read the same value and both store value+1, losing increments. add_created and add_error correctly use fetch_add, so the resolved count undercounts under load.

findings.title: stats() divides by the link count without a zero check
findings.description: `let per_link = hits / guard.len() as i64;` panics on integer division by zero when the store is empty, which is the state of a freshly started server. A GET /stats on an empty store crashes the handler.

findings.title: success_rate() divides before multiplying, truncating to 0
findings.description: `(used / self.links.len() * 100)` performs the integer division first. Whenever `used < links.len()` the quotient is 0, so the rate is reported as 0% unless every single link was hit.

findings.title: validate() collects problems but always returns Ok
findings.description: `validate` pushes error strings for a bad port or zero timeout and prints them, but unconditionally returns `Ok(())`. main.rs:32 relies on `.unwrap()` to reject a bad deploy, which can never happen. A garbage LINKD_PORT becomes port 0 (bind picks an arbitrary port) and a bad LINKD_TIMEOUT_MS becomes a 0 timeout (config.rs:45), yet the server still starts.

findings.title: LINKD_CACHE_TTL_MS is applied as seconds, not milliseconds
findings.description: The doc (config.rs:30-31) says LINKD_CACHE_TTL_MS is a duration in milliseconds, but the code does `Duration::from_secs(n)`. A configured 300000 (intended 300 s) becomes 300000 s (~3.5 days) — 1000x too large.

findings.title: count_by_owner() locks the store Mutex twice, deadlocking
findings.description: It takes `store.lock()` into `guard`, then, while still holding it, calls `store.lock()` again for `second`. std::sync::Mutex is not reentrant, so the second lock blocks forever — a guaranteed deadlock on any call. It also returns the total `len()`, not a per-owner count.

findings.title: require_admin() rejects every role
findings.description: `if session.role != 'admin' || session.role != 'owner'` is always true (a role cannot equal both strings), so the function always returns Err.

findings.title: delete() does not return the owner's quota slot
findings.description: The doc says delete gives the owner their quota slot back, but the body only does `let _ = link.owner;` and never decrements `self.quota`. Quota counts are incremented on create and only grow, so a user who deletes links is left with an inflated count (which, if quotas were ever enforced, would block re-creation).

findings.title: write_snapshot() ignores the rename result
findings.description: `let _ = fs::rename(&tmp, ...)` discards the outcome, so the function returns Ok even when the snapshot was never moved into place (a cross-filesystem rename from /tmp fails). It also uses a fixed /tmp path, so concurrent snapshots collide, and it never syncs the file before renaming, so the 'bytes on disk' guarantee is not met.

findings.title: rename() validates from twice and never validates to
findings.description: `validate_code(from)?;` appears on both line 70 and line 71; the destination code `to` is never validated, so a rename to a code that is too short, too long, or contains invalid characters is accepted.

findings.title: by_owner() matches by substring, not equality
findings.description: `l.owner.contains(owner)` is a substring test: owner 'ali' matches 'alice', 'ali_b', 'malika'; an empty owner matches every link. The doc says 'exactly this owner'.

findings.title: prune() returns the remaining count, not the removed count
findings.description: The doc says prune reports how many links it removed, but it returns `self.links.len()` after retaining — the number left, not the number removed. `before` is captured and then discarded.

findings.title: top() returns the least-followed links
findings.description: `sort_by(|a, b| a.hits.cmp(&b.hits))` sorts ascending (fewest hits first) and `truncate(n)` keeps the head, so it returns the n least-followed links, least first. The doc promises the n most-followed, most hits first.

findings.title: extend() revives already-expired links
findings.description: `extend` sets `expires_at = now + ttl` unconditionally. Its doc says an already-expired link must stay expired ('a dead code must never come back to life'), but this call moves a dead link's expiry into the future and revives it.

findings.title: warm_cache() does not wait for its probes to finish
findings.description: It spawns one thread per pair, then `let _ = handles;` drops the JoinHandles, detaching the threads. The doc says it 'Returns after every probe has finished', but it returns immediately.

findings.title: LINKD_FETCH_LIMIT is parsed then discarded
findings.description: The block parses `limit` then does `let _ = limit;`, never assigning it to `cfg.fetch_limit`, so LINKD_FETCH_LIMIT has no effect (and the field is unused downstream anyway).

findings.title: utilization() can divide by zero and truncates the percentage
findings.description: `guard.len() / self.limit * 100` divides by `self.limit`, which is 0 when LINKD_CACHE_SIZE=0, a division-by-zero panic on GET /stats (main.rs:207). Even when non-zero, `len / limit` is 0 for a mostly-empty cache, so the percentage is almost always 0.

findings.title: count_by_owner deadlocks: locks the same Mutex twice in one thread
findings.description: store.lock() is called on line 120 and again on line 122 while the first guard is still alive. std::sync::Mutex is not reentrant, so the second call blocks forever on a lock the same thread already holds. Any call to count_by_owner hangs the calling thread permanently: a handler thread means a stuck connection, the janitor means the expiry sweep dies forever. It has no caller today, but it is the pub API behind the quota dashboard.

findings.title: ABBA deadlock between Cache::get and Cache::flush
findings.description: get() holds the entries write lock (line 33) and then takes the hits lock (line 45); flush() takes hits first (line 116) and then the entries write lock (line 117). Interleaving: a resolver thread in get() holds entries(write) and waits for hits; a flush caller holds hits and waits for entries(write). Neither can proceed - a certain deadlock that hangs the resolver and the flush. Both are pub methods (flush is documented as serving the admin flush endpoint).

findings.title: Metrics::add_resolved loses increments: non-atomic load/store
findings.description: Unlike add_created and add_error (which use fetch_add), add_resolved does a Relaxed load then a store of current+1. Two handler threads (redirect and out both call it) can interleave load(5)/store(6)/load(5)/store(6), silently dropping one increment. Under concurrent traffic the 'resolved' counter reported by /stats undercounts, worse the longer and heavier the load.

findings.title: Dropping JanitorStop does not stop the janitor thread
findings.description: The doc at line 50 promises the handle 'stops the sweep when it is dropped', but there is no Drop impl: dropping the handle drops the mpsc::Sender, after which try_recv().is_ok() in the loop (line 54) is false forever on the disconnected channel, so the janitor thread keeps running - a leaked thread that keeps locking the store and sweeping the cache. Additionally, even an explicit stop() is only observed at the top of the loop before sleep, so shutdown lags by up to the full interval (60s).

findings.title: warm_cache returns before probes finish: JoinHandles dropped without join
findings.description: One thread is spawned per pair, then 'let _ = handles;' drops the handles. Dropping a JoinHandle does not wait for the thread, so warm_cache returns while the cache.set probes are still running, violating the documented 'Returns after every probe has finished'. A caller that proceeds assuming the cache is primed sees a cold or half-evicted cache (its sets race with other eviction/warm callers). The per-pair thread spawn is also unbounded.

findings.title: Global store mutex held across blocking socket and disk I/O
findings.description: Every handler holds self.store.lock() live across respond/redirect_to, which do blocking writes to the client socket: create_link (124), redirect (140), list_links (156), admin_quotas (190), stats (197); report (215) additionally holds it across export_csv/read_report disk I/O. TcpStream::write blocks when the client stops reading, so one stalled or slow client pins the only store lock: every other connection's create/resolve/list/stats and the janitor's 60s sweep (worker.rs:59) queue behind it, stalling the entire service until the client goes away. (Paths are currently gated behind a session that no endpoint can issue; the hazard is real the moment auth is wired.)

findings.title: Panic under the store lock permanently poisons the mutex and bricks every thread
findings.description: Handlers panic while holding the store guard: stats computes hits / guard.len() as i64, which is division by zero on a fresh (empty) store; and Store::page (store.rs:88-92) sets end = all.len() + 1 and then slices all[offset..end], out of bounds whenever 0 < len < offset+size - e.g. report's page(0, 1000) with fewer than 1000 links, or list_links' default size 20 with 1..19 links. Dropping the guard during unwind permanently poisons the mutex, and every subsequent store.lock().unwrap() in every thread then panics: all store endpoints, and the janitor (worker.rs:59), whose death also stops the expiry sweep forever. One request bricks the service until restart (reachable once a session can be issued).

findings.title: Unbounded thread-per-connection with no read timeout
findings.description: main spawns one OS thread per accepted connection (line 55) and immediately does a blocking read_to_end (line 66) with no read deadline and no cap on concurrent connections. A client that connects and sends nothing - or trickles one byte at a time - pins that thread indefinitely, so a slowloris-style peer grows the thread count without bound until the process exhausts memory/threads. Reachable without authentication, since the read happens before the token check.

findings.title: Cache::sweep can delete a fresh entry: check-then-act TOCTOU
findings.description: sweep collects expired codes under a read lock (94-102), drops it (104), then deletes each code one at a time under write locks (105). In that gap another thread's set (e.g. a warm_cache probe) can re-insert the same code with a fresh TTL; sweep's delayed delete then removes the fresh, non-expired entry. Consequence: valid cached targets are invalidated (extra store lookups) and the documented contract - 'drops every expired entry' - is violated because a non-expired one was dropped.

findings.title: Session tokens are generated from a time-seeded LCG (predictable)
findings.description: issue() mints the 32-hex-char session token from a 64-bit linear congruential generator seeded with SystemTime::now().as_secs() (second resolution), then 16 deterministic iterations. Given an approximate issue time, an attacker can reproduce the exact token and impersonate that user/role (full auth bypass). The doc comment claims the token is 'unguessable' but no CSPRNG is used and the output is fully deterministic from wall-clock time. (issue currently has no caller, so this is latent until token issuance is wired up — but it is the credential-minting primitive, and the bug ships with the feature.)

findings.title: Admin endpoint gated only on a client-supplied x-admin header
findings.description: admin_quotas is documented as 'Administrators only' but its only gate is headers.get("x-admin") == "true". Every request already carries a valid session (auth is enforced in handle before dispatch), so any user can add the header and read the admin-only per-owner quota data. The real check (Authenticator::require_admin) is never called, and is itself broken: `role != "admin" || role != "owner"` is true for every role, so it always rejects. This is a vertical privilege escalation via an authorization decision made from untrusted client input.

findings.title: Path traversal / arbitrary file write via report ?name=
findings.description: report() passes the user-controlled ?name= straight into export_csv, which builds `Path::new(dir).join(format!("{}.csv", name))` and fs::write's it. `name` is never validated. A relative `../../x` climbs out of export_dir, and an absolute `name` is honored by Path::join (the absolute second argument replaces the base), so the service user can create or overwrite an arbitrary *.csv file anywhere it can write (e.g. name=/etc/... -> /etc/... .csv). The doc comment claims the name 'is confined to dir' — it is not. Concrete consequence: corrupt/overwrite other data files or plant a file for further compromise.

findings.title: HTTP response splitting / header injection via CRLF in stored target
findings.description: redirect_to() writes the target directly into the Location header line: `Location: {location}\r\n...`. create_link stores the target verbatim (parse_query does no URL-decoding or CRLF stripping, and the body is taken raw via read_to_end), so a target like `http://x\r\nSet-Cookie: pwn=1` passes the starts_with("http://") check and is stored. On GET /l?code=... the 302 response then carries the attacker-injected `Set-Cookie` (or any other, e.g. a second response) header. This is concrete header injection / response splitting on the public redirect endpoint.

findings.title: No token-issuance path exists; authentication can never succeed
findings.description: Authenticator::issue is the only thing that populates sessions, but it has no caller anywhere. Therefore sessions is always empty, verify() (main.rs:93) always fails, and every request either panics in bearer_token (missing/malformed Authorization header) or returns 401. The gated endpoints are unreachable in the current build, which means none of the downstream access controls are actually exercised. Fixing issuance without fixing the other findings in this review would expose them all.

findings.title: Open redirect on /out via unvalidated ?next=
findings.description: out() returns `301 Location: {next}` where next is taken from ?next= with no scheme or host validation. `?next=https://evil.com` (or `//evil.com`, `javascript:`, `data:`) redirects the client off-site under the trusted shortener origin — a classic open redirect usable for phishing. It is intended as a redirector, but the destination is never constrained.

findings.title: Link owner is taken from the request body, not the session
findings.description: create_link derives owner from fields.get("owner") (client-controlled), not from the authenticated session, so any authenticated user can create links attributed to an arbitrary owner — spoofing identity and consuming that owner's quota. delete_link's doc comment claims the owner is 'taken from the authenticated session,' but no session field is used for ownership anywhere in the write path.

findings.title: bearer_token panics on missing/malformed Authorization header
findings.description: bearer_token does parts[1] on header.split(' '). A request with no Authorization header (authorization = "") or `Authorization: Bearer` with no token yields fewer than 2 parts, so parts[1] is an index-out-of-bounds panic in the handler thread. This is reached on every unauthenticated request at main.rs:92, so a trivial request crashes the connection handler (availability/DoS). This path is reachable in the current build, before any token check.

findings.title: Session token is written to stdout logs
findings.description: issue() prints the freshly minted token: [REDACTED]"auth: issued token {} for {}", session.token, owner). These are 12-hour credentials; writing them to logs (and any log shipper/aggregator) leaks working tokens. Separately, the 401 handler echoes the presented token back in the response body (main.rs:98). (Latent: the println is in the issue path, which is currently unwired.)

findings.title: create() panics for any new owner (uninitialized quota)
findings.description: create() does `*self.quota.get_mut(owner).unwrap() += 1`, but the quota map is never pre-populated, so the first create for any owner hits None.unwrap() and panics. The core write path (POST /links) therefore crashes the handler for every user. The link is also inserted into self.links on line 47 before the panic, leaving an orphaned entry with no HTTP response ever sent.

findings.title: Password 'hash' is unsalted djb2 (fast, unkeyed, 64-bit)
findings.description: hash_password is unsalted djb2: a fast, unkeyed, 64-bit non-cryptographic hash. It is trivially rainbow-tabled and brute-forced and provides no salting, keying, or iteration — wholly unsuitable for storing user passwords. Currently has no caller, so this is latent.

findings.title: secret_eq claims constant-time but returns early (timing leak)
findings.description: secret_eq is documented as a constant-time comparison, but it returns immediately on a length mismatch and on the first differing byte, leaking the length of the common prefix via response timing — the exact side channel it claims to prevent. Currently has no caller; it is the wrong primitive if intended for token/secret comparison.

findings.title: CORS wildcard origin combined with credentials
findings.description: respond() sets Access-Control-Allow-Origin: * together with Access-Control-Allow-Credentials: true. That combination is invalid per the CORS spec (browsers refuse to honor credentials with a wildcard), but it signals a permissive cross-origin policy on a service that returns authenticated data; if the wildcard is ever replaced with the reflected request origin, credentialed cross-origin reads become possible.

findings.title: resolve() expiry check is inverted; expired links stay live
findings.description: resolve() computes `expired = SystemTime::now() < link.expires_at`, which is backwards: a not-yet-expired link is treated as expired (removed and returns None, so a valid link is destroyed on its first click), while an already-expired link (now > expires_at) keeps resolving and counting hits. Security consequence: links meant to be time-limited remain resolvable past their expiry.

findings.title: Plaintext HTTP on 0.0.0.0 exposes tokens and data in transit
findings.description: The server binds 0.0.0.0 and speaks plain HTTP with no TLS. Bearer tokens (the auth credential) and all link data cross the network in cleartext on every interface; a network observer can capture valid tokens and impersonate users or read/modify link data.

findings.title: page() off-by-one panics whenever the requested page extends past the end
findings.description: page() sets `end = all.len() + 1` when offset+size > all.len(), then slices all[offset..end]. That end index exceeds the vector length, so the slice panics. This triggers in the common case (e.g. GET /links?offset=0&size=20 with fewer than 20 links), crashing the list handler. (Reachable once token issuance is wired up.)
